samples.summary: Loopback callback rejects any request carrying an `Origin` header, which can refuse the genuine browser redirect and hang login for the full timeout
samples.evidence: `if (req.method !== 'GET' || req.headers.origin !== undefined) { refuse(res, 403, REFUSAL.notNavigation); return; }` — the genuine flow is a cross-origin 302 from the backend to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`. Most browsers omit `Origin` on GET navigations, but some UAs/extensions/privacy tools attach `Origin` (sometimes `Origin: null`) on cross-origin *redirected* navigations. If any does, every real callback is refused, the wait never settles, and `login` fails only after 30 s. A refusal here is unrecoverable for that user/browser combination, unlike the nonce checks which at least have an alternate path. The header check also blocks HEAD requests, which some tools issue before GET.

samples.summary: `callbackPromise` is created eagerly and can reject before any handler is attached, turning a login timeout into an unhandled rejection
samples.evidence: `const callbackPromise = new Promise<string>(...)` is constructed inside `startCallbackServer`, while the only `.catch`/`await` is attached later at line 54 (`code = await waitForCallback()`), after `await import('open')` and `await open(oauthUrl)`. If those take longer than `options.timeoutMs` (150 ms in the new tests, 30 s in production) the timeout at line 338 calls `callbackReject(...)` on a promise with no handler — Node reports an unhandled rejection (fatal by default in modern Node) instead of the intended `loginTimeoutMessage`. New tests such as login.test.ts's 150 ms cases narrow the window considerably.

samples.summary: `--dry-run` paths bypass the new `parseOutputFormat` guard, so `--format bogus` succeeds with exit 0 on some commands and fails on others
samples.evidence: In `files rename`/`files delete` (lines 124-131, 145-150), `notes`/`slides`/`docs` rename+delete, and `cells batch` (cells.ts:147 dry-run block precedes the `parseOutputFormat` at cells.ts:158), the dry-run branch returns before the format is validated. Meanwhile `docs create` (docs.ts:101) and `notes create` (notes.ts:61) validate *before* the dry-run branch. So `wafflebase files rename doc-1 X --dry-run --format bogus` exits 0 while `wafflebase docs create X --dry-run --format bogus` exits 1 with INVALID_FORMAT — inconsistent contract for the same invalid flag, and a dry run cannot be used to pre-validate the real invocation.

samples.summary: `--format csv` now emits values that no longer equal the `--format json` values (leading `'`), breaking format-agreement consumers
samples.evidence: `neutralizeFormula` prefixes `'` to any value starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, tab or CR (unless a plain number), and `format()` passes `neutralizeFormulas: true` for the whole `--format csv` render path. `scripts/agent/charters/round-trip.md:19` asserts "the same data under `--format json` and `--format csv` agrees"; after this change `sheets cells get <doc> --format csv` returns `'=SUM(A1)` where JSON returns `=SUM(A1)`. Any consumer that piped `--format csv` output back into the API now writes literal text. Intentional and documented in docs/design/cli.md:880, but the divergence is silent at the data level.

samples.summary: `parseCliNonce` silently drops an out-of-range nonce, causing the CLI to report a misleading "server is older than this CLI" diagnosis
samples.evidence: `/^[0-9a-f]{32,128}$/` — any nonce outside 32-128 lowercase hex chars (e.g. a shorter or uppercase nonce from a differently-built CLI) is dropped to `undefined`, so auth.controller.ts:131 omits `&state=`, and the CLI then refuses with `REFUSAL.noState` whose text asserts the *server* is out of date. The real cause (a nonce the server rejected as malformed) is never reported anywhere, making the failure undiagnosable from either side.

samples.summary: The missing-`code` 400 branch does not record `lastRefusal`, so that failure is invisible in the timeout message
samples.evidence: `if (!code) { res.writeHead(400); res.end('Missing code'); return; }` returns without setting `lastRefusal`, unlike every other rejection path which goes through `refuse()`. A callback that arrives with an error (e.g. the OAuth provider redirecting without a code) therefore still ends in the bare `Login timed out.` message the new code was written to avoid.

finding.summary: Loopback callback rejects any request carrying an `Origin` header, which can refuse the genuine browser redirect and hang login for the full timeout
finding.evidence: `if (req.method !== 'GET' || req.headers.origin !== undefined) { refuse(res, 403, REFUSAL.notNavigation); return; }` — the genuine flow is a cross-origin 302 from the backend to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback`. Most browsers omit `Origin` on GET navigations, but some UAs/extensions/privacy tools attach `Origin` (sometimes `Origin: null`) on cross-origin *redirected* navigations. If any does, every real callback is refused, the wait never settles, and `login` fails only after 30 s. A refusal here is unrecoverable for that user/browser combination, unlike the nonce checks which at least have an alternate path. The header check also blocks HEAD requests, which some tools issue before GET.

verdict.reason: The guard is present as quoted (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:267-270), but it cannot fire on the genuine flow. The backend answers GitHub's top-level GET at @Get('github/callback') with an Express 302 to http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:97, 134-136), so the browser follows it as a top-level GET navigation. Per the Fetch standard the Origin header is appended only for cors-tainted requests, websocket mode, or methods other than GET/HEAD (the cross-origin-redirect `Origin: null` rule is inside that non-safe-method branch), so a redirected GET navigation carries no Origin in conforming UAs — a point the finding itself concedes. The claimed unrecoverable 30 s hang therefore requires a hypothetical spec-violating UA rather than an actual path in this repo. The secondary HEAD claim is also non-blocking: refuse() (login.ts:240-249) only writes a 403 and records lastRefusal, never touching `settled`/`callbackResolve` (login.ts:329-332), so a stray HEAD probe leaves the wait open and the following genuine GET still resolves — the repo's own test demonstrates exactly this keep-waiting behavior for the sibling refusal branches (packages/cli/test/login.test.ts:55-79).

mergedFrom.summary: Blanket `Origin` header rejection can refuse the genuine browser redirect, breaking every login

finding.summary: Callback server rejects any request carrying an `Origin` header, which risks refusing the genuine browser redirect on browsers/proxies that attach one
finding.evidence: `if (req.method !== 'GET' || req.headers.origin !== undefined) { 403 }`. The real callback arrives as a cross-origin 302 redirect from the backend; if any browser, extension, or corporate proxy attaches an `Origin` (e.g. `Origin: null` on cross-origin redirect chains), the legitimate code is refused and, because the 403 branch deliberately never settles the promise (line 227-233), `waitForCallback()` hangs until the 30s timeout and login fails with a timeout error the user cannot diagnose. Only node `fetch` (which never sets Origin unless asked) is exercised in packages/cli/test/login.test.ts.

verdict.reason: The condition is present verbatim at packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:267 (`req.method !== 'GET' || req.headers.origin !== undefined` -> 403), and the refusal path (refuse(), lines 240-249) intentionally never settles the callback promise, so the only other exit is the 30s timeout at lines 335-341, which rejects waitForCallback() (used at line 54) and fails login. The genuine callback is a cross-origin redirect chain — backend issues res.redirect('http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?...') at packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:134-136 after a redirect from github.com — and an Origin header (typically `Origin: null` after a tainted-origin form POST such as GitHub's Authorize button) is not stripped by a 302 method change, so a legitimate callback can plausibly carry Origin and be refused. No guard, fallback, retry, or `null`-Origin exemption exists anywhere in the file, and the tests only cover forged Origins (packages/cli/test/login.test.ts:81-93, 123-133) while all happy-path requests use node fetch with no Origin (lines 46, 72, 86). Real, reachable, and it breaks a core flow (login) — blocking under the correctness rubric.
